data.title: Trump says GOP voters 'angry' at congressional Republicans ahead of midterms but not at him
data.description:
President Trump in an interview aired early Friday appeared to deflect blame for the anger among the Republican base toward the party’s leadership in Congress, saying in an interview published early Friday GOP voters are not “angry” with his job as president. 

“They’re angry at Republicans but they’re not angry at me,” Trump told Punchbowl News. 

Trump said the question for Republicans ahead of the midterms is if the party’s base will turn out to vote in November when he is not at the top of the ballot. 

“That’s the one thing I can’t tell [you]. I’m going to ask them to,” the president continued. 

“The question is will they vote because a lot of them are very angry at Republicans,” he said. 

A slew of recent polls show Trump with low approval ratings, which could threaten Republicans running in midterm races. 

A Quinnipiac University poll released last week found that only 32 percent of all registered voters said they support how Trump has handled his second term in office.

A separate CNN survey released last week showed Democrats leading Republicans on the generic ballot by 8 points. The Decision Desk HQ polling average currently has Democrats leading Republicans by just over 6 points. 

While Trump has recently clashed with some Republicans on Capitol Hill, particularly in the Senate, the president has recently hit the campaign trail to bolster GOP enthusiasm ahead of the midterms. 

Trump rallied supporters at an event highlighting the “No Taxes on Tips” provision of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in Las Vegas on Wednesday. 

Updated at 7:40 a.m. EDT

data.title: Our current housing crisis began in 2008 — and it never ended
data.description:
America’s housing crisis has been rightly blamed on a lack of supply. Lately the finger has been pointed at inflation as the driving force behind it.

Some evidence seems to support that notion. Home prices remain stubbornly high. Mortgage rates have more than doubled from their pandemic lows. Insurance premiums are soaring. Construction costs continue to rise, and rents consume an ever-larger share of household budgets.

But inflation did not create America’s housing crisis. It only exposed it.

To understand why millions of Americans are struggling to find housing they can afford, we need to look beyond the economic headlines of the last few years and revisit a crisis that began nearly two decades ago, in the wreckage of the Global Financial Crisis.

When the housing market collapsed in 2008, the damage extended far beyond foreclosures and failing banks. Homebuilders went out of business. Construction workers left the industry. Lending tightened dramatically. Investment dried up. Housing production fell off a cliff.

The economy eventually recovered, but housing production never did. In fact, the 2010s saw the fewest single-family home construction starts since at least the 1960s and nearly half as many as the decade that preceded it.

Now, Freddie Mac estimates the nation is short by about 3.7 million homes of what is needed to meet demand. The National Low Income Housing Coalition estimates that there is a shortage of 7.2 million rental homes affordable to renters with incomes at or below the federal poverty guideline.

A recent report from my organization’s National Housing Strategic Initiatives team notes that housing production dropped considerably in the aftermath of the financial crisis and “has failed to catch up with current demand.” The report argues that the effects of the housing crash continue to echo throughout today’s market, helping to drive the affordability challenges confronting households across the country.

That observation should fundamentally change how we think about housing affordability.

While the conventional narrative treats today’s crisis as a recent phenomenon driven by inflation, interest rates, or pandemic-era disruptions, those factors are really accelerants poured onto a fire that was already burning.

The reality is that the nation entered the pandemic with a severe housing shortage that had been accumulating for more than a decade.

When demand surged and borrowing costs fell during the pandemic, there was little available supply to absorb it. Prices climbed as families found themselves bidding against one another for an increasingly limited number of homes.

Now, as inflation and higher interest rates put additional pressure on the market, the shortage created after 2008 is becoming even more visible. It is perhaps best seen through the perspective of affordable housing providers. Unlike market-rate developers, affordable housing operators often have limited ability to raise rents to offset rising expenses, even though they are confronting many of the same economic pressures affecting the broader market.

According to the report, operating costs for affordable housing have increased dramatically in recent years, with insurance spiking more than 110 percent, and repairs and maintenance costs climbing 35 percent since 2017.

Meanwhile, multifamily housing starts have slowed, affordable housing shortages persist, and hundreds of thousands of existing affordable units are expected to see affordability restrictions expire in the years ahead.

These are serious challenges, and for years policymakers have debated housing affordability through the lens of monthly costs. They argue about mortgage rates, rent caps, insurance premiums, property taxes, zoning regulations, environmental reviews, institutional investors, and short-term economic trends. But the fact is, the country simply stopped building enough housing after 2008 and never made up the difference.

We must recognize that there is no way to fix this overnight, but there are solutions. First, we must start viewing housing as part of our essential economic infrastructure. A functioning economy depends on workers of all types — teachers, nurses, first responders — being able to afford to live near their jobs. Economic mobility depends on families having access to stable and affordable housing.

With that mindset, policymakers, investors, and housing organizations can then work together to strengthen the housing ecosystem, including by expanding access to capital, supporting nonprofit and emerging housing developers, preserving existing affordable housing stock, modernizing financing tools, and advancing federal, state, and local policies that encourage housing production and preservation.

The Great Recession officially ended in 2009, but the housing recession never did.

Until policymakers address the structural housing deficit that emerged from the financial crisis, Americans will continue to experience the consequences through higher rents, higher home prices, and fewer opportunities to achieve economic security.

Inflation may be today’s villain. But the story began long before inflation arrived.

Valerie White is head of National Housing Strategic Initiatives for Local Initiatives Support Corporation.

data.title: Beijing may be adapting its influence playbook for America's infrastructure debate
data.description:
The race for artificial intelligence is often described as a competition over semiconductors, foundation models and talent. Increasingly, however, it is also becoming a competition over something far less glamorous: electricity, transmission lines, and the data centers that power modern AI.

That shift has implications far beyond industrial policy. It is also reshaping how China influences public debate inside the U.S.

For years, U.S. policymakers have focused on defending against Chinese cyber espionage, intellectual property theft, and influence campaigns aimed at Washington. Yet as federal institutions have become harder targets, Beijing’s information operations appear to be evolving. Rather than trying to persuade Americans to support China directly, recent evidence suggests a growing emphasis on amplifying existing domestic disagreements around strategically important industries.

Earlier this year, a report by OpenAI explained how the company disrupted a Chinese-linked influence operation that used ChatGPT to generate fabricated social media posts opposing American AI data centers. The campaign dubbed ”Data Center Bandwagon” created fake American personas arguing that data centers would dramatically increase electricity bills and harm local communities. OpenAI traced the activity to a private Chinese technology company working for provincial government clients.

By itself, the operation was relatively modest, producing just a handful of fake accounts. But that misses the larger strategic significance. The campaign illustrates an important evolution in Chinese influence. Rather than promoting overtly pro-Beijing narratives, the operators sought to insert themselves into an already contentious American policy debate. Instead of inventing new grievances, they amplified existing ones by creating fake local voices designed to appear authentic.

This reflects a broader trend visible across multiple recent investigations. Graphika documented “Spamouflage” networks posing as Americans across the political spectrum ahead of the 2024 election. Microsoft Threat Intelligence likewise found that Chinese influence operations have become increasingly sophisticated, experimenting with fabricated personas and targeting politically salient issues.

OpenAI’s findings indicate those same techniques are now being applied to one of the most important domestic debates of the decade: whether and where America should build the infrastructure needed to compete in the AI race.

Data centers are rapidly becoming critical national infrastructure. They underpin frontier AI development, cloud computing, advanced manufacturing, military applications, and scientific research.

The U.S. and China increasingly view AI leadership as a central determinant of economic and military competitiveness. Chinese state media has criticized American data centers as environmentally damaging and economically costly, yet the Chinese government  continues to subsidize domestic AI infrastructure. China’s own electricity demand from data centers is projected to more than double by 2030.

None of this demonstrates that China singlehandedly created America’s debate over AI infrastructure. Nor does it suggest that local opposition to data centers is somehow illegitimate. Communities across the country are raising genuine concerns about energy demand, water consumption, land use, and quality of life. This distinction is important. Some reporting has questioned broader claims about coordinated Chinese involvement in domestic anti-data-center activism and emphasized that many local campaigns are rooted in authentic community concerns.

Foreign influence operations do not need to manufacture domestic disagreements from scratch. They succeed by identifying authentic social and political tensions and selectively amplifying them when doing so advances strategic objectives. This dynamic has been observed across multiple information campaigns, where state-linked actors seek to insert themselves into existing debates rather than invent entirely new ones.

In 2022, Mandiant documented Operation Dragonbridge, a Chinese state-linked campaign that posed as local Texans opposing construction of a Pentagon-supported rare earth processing facility. Google has since removed more than 175,000 Dragonbridge-related accounts across YouTube and Blogger.

The target appears to be changing. Yesterday it was rare earth processing. Today it may be AI infrastructure. Tomorrow it could be transmission lines, semiconductor fabs, quantum computing facilities, or advanced manufacturing plants. The common thread is not the issue itself but the strategy of embedding Beijing’s preferred outcomes within what appears to be authentic American political discourse.

The United States cannot and should not treat every local protest or online criticism as foreign manipulation. Democracies depend upon robust public debate, particularly when major industrial projects reshape communities. But China has no place inauthentically spinning up more anti-data center sentiment, especially while it is encouraging the massive build out in their own country. Its campaign — disparate and clumsy as it may be — aims at slowing down America’s infrastructure build out, exacerbating domestic discussions and fueling policy disagreements on all levels.

The challenge is therefore not eliminating disagreement. It is becoming better at distinguishing between genuine democratic debate and coordinated foreign efforts designed to amplify existing divisions around strategically important technologies.

Nikolas Foster is a nonresident fellow with the Atlantic Council’s Global China Hub and previously served as deputy China advisor to the administrator of USAID.

data.title: Tariff refunds boost quarterly earnings for some of biggest US companies
data.description:
Tariff refunds are showing up on Wall Street. 

The latest quarter spanned the Trump administration handing back the bulk of the $100 billion returned so far. It’s providing many companies a boost as they report their earnings. 

Amazon reported receiving $600 million. Apple said tariff refunds added $0.11 in diluted earnings per share for the quarter. PepsiCo told investors that refunds were helping offset higher commodity costs. Caterpillar said its refunds boosted its operating profit margin higher than anticipated. 

They are among the mega-cap names reaping the benefits after sitting out the legal fight. And tariff refunds extend well beyond tech, as an array of industries try to recoup billions they paid the invalidated tariffs.

Even as the refund amount crosses the $100 billion mark, not all the tariffs have been returned. The government estimates the deposits amount to $166 billion in total.

Small businesses and Democratic-led states were the ones to defeat Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs at the Supreme Court. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce filed an outside brief in support, but backing from large corporations was scant.

Once the high court’s 6-3 ruling invalidating Trump’s tariff landed, it sparked a massive refund process from small and big businesses alike.

“The tariff refunds comes, obviously, very handy and in some other trade-offs that we have to make in the business,” PepsiCo CEO Ramon Laguarta said on the company’s earnings call last month.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection said in an update on Tuesday that $100 billion in refunds has been sent for disbursement so far since it launched its online refund system, known as CAPE.

“The CAPE program has been a remarkable success,” U.S. Court of International Trade Judge Richard Eaton, an appointee of former President Clinton overseeing the refund process, said at a Thursday hearing.

Apple’s CFO attributed $0.11 of diluted earnings per share last quarter to tariff refunds. 

At Amazon, Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Brian Olsavsky said on the company’s earnings call last week that it has received $600 million.

“We are participating in the tariff refund process,” Olsavsky said.

The earnings reports have cast aside any lingering doubt that the companies may hold off on recouping tariffs they paid. 

Trump has repeatedly expressed frustration with the courts’ mandate to refund importers, and in April, he rejoiced at reports suggesting Apple and Amazon wouldn’t participate.

“I think it’s brilliant if they don’t do that,” Trump told CNBC at the time. “Actually, if they don’t do that, they’ve got to know me very well.” 

“If they don’t do that, I’ll remember them,” Trump said.

An Amazon spokesperson declined to comment. Apple did not return The Hill’s request for comment.

As Apple last week pointed to its in-hand refund, Apple CEO Tim Cook emphasized the company’s 12-figure commitment for new domestic investments.

“We plan to reinvest the tariff refunds we’ve received into the U.S,” Cook reminded investors on the earnings call. “We’re pleased with the progress we’ve already made advancing the American supply chain.” 

Still, any boost to the companies’ stock valuations from tariff refunds was dwarfed by investors’ focus on the AI boom and companies’ capital spending. Amazon’s stock surged on its cloud-computing sales growth, while Apple’s fell over a weaker-than-expected revenue growth forecast.

Johnson & Johnson CFO Joseph Wolk highlighted refunds as a reason for improvement in the healthcare giant’s pre-tax operating margin. 

“We now expect approximately a 75-basis point improvement, supported by continuing operating efficiencies and anticipated reduction and recoupment of certain tariff-related costs based on the latest rulings,” Wolk said on the company’s July 15 earnings call. 

PepsiCo CFO Steve Schmitt told investors on its earnings call that refund claims would amount to about 1 full point of earnings-per-share growth for the year. 

“We expect a gradual improvement in North America,” Schmitt said, “and we will be using the tariff, essentially the refunds, to help offset some commodity inflation that we’re seeing and allow us to continue to play offense in the business.” 

Still, executives are cautioning the refunds are only a one-time bump. Companies are still grappling with Trump’s new waves of global tariffs he imposed after the Supreme Court’s ruling. Those are the subject of ongoing litigation. 

In each round of tariffs, large corporations haven’t led the charge. The cases bear the names of small businesses like wine importer VOS Selections, educational toy company Learning Resources and spice business Burlap & Barrel. Blue states have also joined the fight, but not mega-cap corporations.

As they now join in to claim refunds, the influx has also led to questions about whether consumers will see any of the money. The government is legally obligated to refund actual importers, not their customers. 

Dozens of lawsuits are popping up across the country alleging it amounts to unjust enrichment, or corporations are somehow otherwise obligated to hand over refunds back to customers. 

Consumers have filed lawsuits against a long list of brands, including Adidas, American Girl, Columbia Sportswear, Dyson, Five Below, General Motors, IKEA, Lululemon, Mattel, Microsoft, Nike, Puma, Ralph Lauren, Stanley Black & Decker, Target and Zara.

Some law firms are involved in bringing multiple actions. Companies are pushing back by saying at least some cases suffer procedural defects and that they’re meritless, anyway. 

“Plaintiff agreed to pay that charge and got exactly what he paid for. At bottom, Plaintiff’s theory would turn vehicle pricing on its head,” lawyers for General Motors wrote this week as they urged a judge to toss a lawsuit from a man concerning a Buick Enclave he says he purchased in February. 

Amazon and FedEx are two of the most prominent companies that have indicated some direct refunds will be passed along.

FedEx told investors in a recent financial report that its cash balance included $800 million being held to refund customers for tariffs.

Olsavsky, Amazon’s CFO, said on the company’s earnings call last week that there are “limited circumstances” where the company could trace specific tariff refunds to customers. 

“When we receive those refunds, we will proactively contact affected customers and automatically issue refunds to them,” Olsavsky said. “Otherwise, like other large retailers, we’ll utilize refunds to continue to invest in low prices for customers.” 

Refunds continue to rise. But lawyers and the trade court judge have acknowledged that some smaller importers won’t take advantage of the system, and it also doesn’t accept claims in some circumstances.

“We are left with the prospect of the Treasury retaining billions of dollars of unlawfully collected duties and tens of thousands of importers being denied refunds they are owed,” said Eaton, the judge, at a Thursday hearing.

He convened the hearing to consider certifying a class action to ensure all refunds go out. Once again, it’s a motion led by small businesses.

data.title: Abuse, harassment allegations threaten to derail Republicans' midterm message
data.description:
House Republicans are confronting an unwelcome political headache as a string of abuse or harassment allegations involving several GOP lawmakers threatens to complicate the party’s midterm message just months before the November elections.

The domestic abuse allegations against Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio), coupled with the scrutiny surrounding Reps. Cory Mills (R-Fla.) and Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.), have dominated headlines and handed Democrats fresh political ammunition at a critical point in the campaign. The developments have also served as an unwelcome distraction for GOP leaders, who have sought to keep voters focused on their message that Republicans are best equipped to tackle inflation, the rising cost of living and other kitchen-table concerns.

The timing is particularly challenging for Republicans as they work to defend their narrow House majority. Although the controversies involve individual lawmakers, the steady stream of negative headlines could have a cumulative effect, forcing vulnerable incumbents to answer for events far outside their own districts. 

“Vulnerable House Republicans mistakenly think that no matter how awful their behavior is, they are untouchable. Voters in these districts are pissed over higher costs, Republicans’ broken promises, and are ready to reject these scandal-plagued members, who’ve made voters’ lives worse. Every single vulnerable Republican who has coddled and stood by these creeps should be ashamed of themselves, are unfit to serve, and will lose their job in November,” Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee spokesperson Viet Shelton told The Hill in a statement.

Douglas Heye, a GOP strategist, said that “Miller and Mills make it harder for Republicans to talk about the issues they want to focus on.”

“The faster they are gone, the better for everyone,” Heye said, arguing that both GOP lawmakers should drop their reelection bids.

Miller, in particular, has been in the hot seat over allegations of domestic abuse leveled by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, with whom he’s been locked in a bitter custody battle. She says that he hurled hot water at her, pointed a gun at her head and may have broken their daughter’s collarbone. The House Ethics Committee is reviewing domestic violence and illegal drug use allegations against him.

Miller has vehemently denied all the claims and remained defiant, vowing to stay in his race while conducting a series of interviews and posting frequent rebuttals online.

Emily Moreno’s father, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), has called for Miller to resign from Congress, and a growing chorus of Moreno’s Senate colleagues are questioning Miller’s decision to stay in the race.

Sen. Bernie Moreno also accused Miller of refusing to return a stuffed blue bunny belonging to Miller’s daughter, a claim that Miller denied but that seemed to strike a chord with many online.

“What kind of person would treat their daughter this way? This guy is clearly a degenerate sociopath,” Sen. Tim Sheehy (R-Mont.) wrote on the social platform X in response.

“Max should step aside and seek help. Staying in this race makes it far more likely we lose this seat and hand Democrats a majority to impeach President Trump,” Sheehy added.

Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), who is competing in one of the toughest Senate races in the country in November, broke his silence on the issue Wednesday to call for Miller to resign and drop out of his race for reelection.

And Donovan O’Neil, state director at Americans for Prosperity-Ohio, wrote on X that Miller is “unfit for office,” arguing that Republicans should call him out and “exorcise our own demons from the GOP.”

Democrats, meanwhile, have wasted no time seizing on the allegations to pressure other Republicans running in tight seats. JoAnna Mendoza, who’s running to represent Arizona’s “toss-up” 6th Congressional District, was quick to target Rep. Juan Ciscomani (R-Ariz.), who she is facing off against in November.

“So… are you going to return the $5,000 you took from Max Miller’s PAC, @JuanCiscomani? Or is he another one of your buddies? If you actually cared about the safety of women and girls, you would speak out about this. But of course, crickets,” she wrote on X.

Miller, however, isn’t the only Republican giving some of his colleagues campaign jitters.

Mills, who is under investigation by the House Ethics Committee over allegations of dating violence and campaign finance law violations, is also running for reelection in his Florida district.

Notably, Reps. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) and Mike Haridopolos (R-Fla.) endorsed GOP candidate Ryan Elijah over Mills in a joint statement Wednesday.

Luna told Politico that Mills “needs to not be seeking reelection.”

A state judge in October granted an ex-girlfriend of Mills a restraining order after she said he harassed her and threatened to release explicit images of her. Another woman Mills was dating simultaneously initially told police he assaulted her in February 2025 before recanting.

Mills has previously faced calls to resign or be expelled. He has denied all allegations of wrongdoing.

But it’s not just Republicans currently on the ballot who are fueling anxiety within the party. Lawmakers who have already resigned or withdrawn their reelection bids amid scandal have also left a lasting mark on the GOP, forcing Republicans to contend with the political fallout.

Edwards dropped his reelection bid earlier this week after the House Ethics Committee recommended he be formally censured following an investigation that found he violated the “spirit” of the chamber’s policies on sexual harassment of staff. 

Edwards’ seat is rated as “lean Republican” by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report.

Rep. Kat Cammack (R-Fla.), chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, called for the House to still follow through with censuring Edwards despite his decision to drop out.

“A resignation announcement does not erase misconduct or absolve a Member of accountability. No one should be permitted to run out the clock and avoid the consequences of their actions,” she said.

And former Rep. Tony Gonzales (R-Texas), who admitted to having an affair with a staffer who died after setting herself on fire, also made headlines earlier this year. He exited Congress in April.

The Hill has reached out to the National Republican Campaign Committee for comment.

To be sure, Democrats have not been immune from serious accusations in their ranks.

Former Rep. Eric Swalwell (D-Calif.) exited Congress in April and dropped out of the California gubernatorial race amid allegations of sexual assault and misconduct. The San Francisco Chronicle published accusations from a former aide that Swalwell sexually assaulted her on two occasions. CNN also reported three other women making separate allegations of sexual misconduct. 

 And Graham Platner withdrew from the Maine Senate race last month after he was accused of sexual assault and sexual misconduct by two women, one of whom alleged he had raped her in 2021. Platner vehemently denied the allegations but was ultimately forced out after his former backers called on him to leave the race.

Even as scrutiny increases on their members, most GOP lawmakers have been mum on whether Miller and Mills should drop out of their races.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) told Politico’s Dasha Burns that he would not tell Miller to drop out.

“I will tell Max what I tell everyone,” he said. “These are serious allegations. I’m the father of two daughters who work on Capitol Hill. I mean, the allegations are serious. I think Max is taking them seriously, I think our colleagues are, but again, we have to allow this process to play out. It’s just begun.”

Asked last month why Miller and Mills haven’t been pushed out of the House GOP, Johnson had pointed to the Ethics Committee process then as well.

Cammack said in a statement that the allegations against Miller are “deeply troubling” and “deserve a fair, thorough review.”

“Due process is not optional—it is how the truth is established and justice is served. This is clearly an evolving situation, with new allegations continuing to emerge, which is all the more reason to let the full process play out and follow the facts wherever they lead. The Ethics Committee is now reviewing these allegations, and I respect that process,” she said. 

“Above all, this is an incredibly painful situation for everyone involved, and my heart especially breaks for the little girl caught in the middle,” she added.

data.title: Trump may be just what Michigan Democrats need after bruising primary
data.description:
Democrats have a unity problem three months out from the general election, after a bruising primary that showed how evenly the party’s voters are split between progressive and centrist visions for its future. 

President Trump may be exactly what they need to pull together and defeat the GOP nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), strategists told The Hill.

Despite their preferred candidate, Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), being defeated by Abdul El-Sayed, the party’s establishment was quick to encourage their base to coalesce behind the progressive former health official, citing the threat of Trump. 

Stevens said in her concession speech that Trump and Rogers “want us to come out of this primary tired and divided,” while Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (D), who had endorsed Stevens, said Rogers and Republicans would be a “rubber stamp for the Trump agenda,” throwing her support behind El-Sayed. 

The congresswoman and the Senate nominee appeared together at a “unity breakfast” for Michigan Democrats on Thursday, even embracing on stage. 

Following his win, El-Sayed set the tone for the party moving forward. 

“Mike Rogers is a guy who, believe it or not, went back to Florida so he can lick every single boot Donald Trump owns to beg for his endorsement,” El-Sayed told supporters following his victory. 

Despite Trump flipping Michigan twice in 2016 and 2024, Democrats say Trump’s poor approval rating, coupled with his handling of the economy, are enough to unite a broad spectrum of voters. 

“Frankly I’m not that worried as long as Abdul talks more about costs and corruption than today’s intraparty fight. Democrats really hate Trump,” said Andrew Mamo, a Democratic operative who has advised candidates this cycle including Mallory McMorrow, who suspended her Senate bid last month. 

Even some Republicans acknowledge the unifying effect Trump has on Democrats of all stripes. 

“They will eat whatever shit sandwich is put in front of them if the end goal is putting a check on Trump in Congress,” said Jason Cable Roe, a Michigan-based Republican strategist. 

Trump’s approval rating in Michigan sits at 37 percent, according to an online tracking poll from Civiqs. By comparison, the president’s approval rating was at 45 percent in the state when he took office in January. 

Democrats also point to Trump’s economic policies, specifically to how they say his tariff policies have wreaked havoc on the state’s economy, which relies largely on auto manufacturing and trade with Canada. 

“The president ran the economy into a ditch with tariffs and a war of choice in the Middle East. As always, Donald Trump is the Sword of Damocles for Republicans: no one turns out voters like Trump, but no one enrages voters like Trump,” said Adrian Hemond, a Michigan-based Democratic consultant. 

But not all Democrats are rushing to unite behind El-Sayed, who has staked out a staunch anti-Israel position. 

“I can’t come together with someone if you are willing to embrace people that love Hamas or that thinks America deserved 9-11. I think that’s reasonable,” Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) said in an interview with CNN on Wednesday. 

The senator, who frequently breaks with his party, was referring to El-Sayed campaigning with left-wing influencer Hassan Piker, who has said he would vote for Hamas over Israel because he is a “lesser evil voter.” Piker said in 2019 that the U.S. “deserved” the September 11th terror attacks, but later acknowledged that the comment was “inappropriate.” 

Fetterman argued El-Sayed’s victory puts the seat more in play for Republicans, and that he could “100 percent” lose to Rogers. 

Recent polling suggests that El-Sayed faces tough fight ahead against Rogers. An EPIC-MRA poll released on Monday just before the primary showed Rogers leading El-Sayed by three points in a head-to-head matchup, within the poll’s four-point margin of error. DDHQ’s election forecast gives El-Sayed a 55 percent chance of prevailing. 

Many Republicans celebrated El-Sayed’s win, saying he was their preferred candidate to run against in the fall. 

“Great news for the Republican Party. El-Sayed, a Communist loser who hates Jews and Israel, is the projected winner in this race with the Socialist,” Trump wrote in a TruthSocial post following news of El-Sayed’s victory. 

The GOP campaign ecosystem has already gone on the offensive against El-Sayed. 

The Senate Leadership Fund rolled out a six-figure digital ad, labeling El-Sayed as “dangerously radical,” while the National Republican Senatorial Committee aired their own ad painting the Democrat in the same light. 

The nastiest attack on El-Sayed yet came on Wednesday from Trump while at an event selling the “No Tax on Tips” provision of the One Big Beautiful Bill in Las Vegas on Wednesday.

“This guy hates Jews,” Trump told a crowd of supporters. “Somebody said, ‘Oh that’s a little strong.’ No, he hates Jews and hates Israel.” 

Some Republicans are wary Trump’s attacks will play into Democrats’ hands. Michigan-based Republican strategist Jason Cable Roe called Trump’s attack on El-Sayed “a mistake.” 

“He is helping Abdul rally the moderates within the Democratic coalition to him because Trump is making this a binary choice between Trump and El-Sayed ,” Roe said.

“Let Mike Rogers run his campaign and stay out of it,” he said. 

The Republican National Committee threw cold water on the prospect of Democrats uniting against Trump in Michigan. 

“Democrats can sing kumbaya all they want, but at the end of the day, their radical candidates’ only message is Trump Derangement Syndrome,” said Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary at the RNC. 

One Michigan Republican strategist echoed the sentiment. 

“It’s quite telling that the only thing that Democrats can seem to agree on is their shared hatred for the President and not a single policy proposal that would actually resonate with voters,” the strategist said. 

Rogers is a formidable opponent in his own right, having only lost to Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) by 19,000 voters in 2024. 

While Roe expressed concern over a potential unifying effect Trump could have on Democrats, he was less concerned about the impact the president would have on Rogers. 

“Trump is baked into the brand,” Roe said. “I don’t think anyone’s going to say ‘oh, I’m not voting for that Republican because they support Trump.” 

Ironically, Trump’s coattails were not long enough for Rogers to take advantage of in Michigan in 2024. Slotkin notably did not invoke Trump during the campaign, instead focusing on economic issues impacting the state. 

Democrats say the difference four years later is that they’re playing offense instead of defense. 

“Trump is so wildly unpopular because of everything he’s done to damage the Michigan economy compared to where he was at that point in 2024,” said one Michigan Democratic strategist. 

“How could people not bring him up?” they said. 

Alyssa Brouillet, communications director for the Rogers campaign, pointed to Tuesday’s results as evidence of the Republicans’ strength heading into November. 

“Michigan Republicans have been unified behind Mike Rogers for over a year and are charging full steam ahead through November,” she said in an emailed statement. “Meanwhile, on Tuesday, Abdul became the only statewide candidate from either party who failed to win support from a majority of voters. More Democrats rejected Abdul than supported him.”

data.title: Iran moves to block US, Israeli shipments from Strait of Hormuz
data.description:
Iranian state media on Thursday reported that Tehran could attempt to block U.S. and Israeli shipments from transiting the Strait of Hormuz under its joint venture with Oman to reopen the critical waterway to commercial traffic. 

Members of Iran’s parliament are reviewing a proposed bill to block “hostile” vessels from moving through the choke point responsible for carrying a fifth of the world’s oil transports per day under normal conditions. 

Ships caught violating the policy could face a 20 percent fine if caught by Iranian authorities, per state media. 

Each ship approved to transit the strait will face fees for insurance, refueling and or environmental costs, according to Iranian state media. 

Although, tolls on international waterways are considered a violation of the principle of freedom of navigation protected under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.

The U.S. and Israel would likely be excluded from all routes after launching joint strikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities last year and again in March, marking the start of a five-month long war that has expanded across the Middle East. 

The Trump administration has considered several off ramps since the start of the war, but all have been unsuccessful as leaders in Tehran and Washington, D.C. accuse one another of violating the agreed upon terms. 

Commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has remained a contentious topic, as Iran attempts to exert full control over the global shipping route by mining the waterway to prevent unwelcome transit. 

American soldiers and Iranian troops worked to demine the strait in June after the signing of a memorandum of understanding that sparked a 60-day ceasefire. However, fighting resumed less than a month later, re-igniting the battle for dominance over the waterway. 

An American naval blockade is currently being imposed in an effort to starve the Iranian regime of oil and trade revenue and exert maximum economic leverage to force a diplomatic resolution and the reopening of the strait free of tolls.

“We control it, but they can always shoot something, they always have something, or drop a mine, and if you have one mine out there you sort of mess things up, because people don’t want to take their billion-dollar boats and accidentally get hit by a mine, but I think we’re doing very well,” Trump told reporters on Thursday, despite Iranian leaders rejecting that narrative. 

The Trump administration has maintained that there will be no tolls on the strait. 

“Any temporary routes will be without any impediments — meaning no approvals or permissions and no tolls or charges. The Strait of Hormuz is an international waterway and no party controls the lanes or the ability to transit through them,” a U.S. official told NPR on condition of anonymity as they were not approved to speak on the record.

As Iran and Oman near a deal to resume commercial traffic in the strait, economists and world leaders are bracing for a potential period of stability for international oil markets rattled by the oscillating war. 

The president said Iran is open to another peace deal and Turkey’s foreign minister on Thursday confirmed an agreement could soon be formed as a result of diplomatic talks.

data.title: Crude oil supplies at 45-year low
data.description:
U.S. crude oil supplies are at a 45-year low as the Iran war continues to tarnish strategic reserves. 

Bank of America Global Research data shows that the level of the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at its lowest level since 1983, leaving the country with 43 days of crude oil supply, as reported by the Associated Press. 

The Trump administration is releasing oil from the reserves to combat rising energy costs sparked by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which carries up to a fifth of the world’s oil transports per day. 

Throughout five months of conflict, the strait has been effectively shut off to commercial traffic, rattling global energy markets and promoting instability for the price of crude oil. 

In response, President Trump committed to a domestic drawdown of 172 million barrels over a 120-day delivery window.

Roughly 108.6 million barrels of crude oil have been released to date, while current inventory levels sit at approximately 304.8 million, according to federal data. 

In June, however, the president warned against relying on strategic reserves to keep the country afloat during war.

“We run out of reserves in about four weeks,” Trump told reporters on June 17. “We would really run out and there’ll be a time when you wouldn’t be able to get it. And do you want to see bedlam?” 

The same day, Trump signed a memorandum of understanding with Iran in an effort to move towards peace in the region. 

The agreement intended to provide a pathway to Iran’s denuclearization and vessels’ safe transit through the Strait of Hormuz for an extended ceasefire, but the deal was short-lived and strikes resumed on July 8.

Crude oil prices surged nearly 5 percent on July 8, and Brent crude rose 5.2 percent, settling at $78.02 a barrel. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude climbed 4.4 percent to $73.52 a barrel. 

South Korea, Thailand, Vietnam and Bangladesh instituted emergency energy rationing and conservation policies such as restricted AC usage or alternate-day driving rules to cope with the fallout. 

China reduced its oil imports from the previous year by roughly 3.5 million barrels per day (BPD), dropping imports from an average of 11 million BPD down to about 7.8 million BPD.

The country has the world’s largest emergency crude oil inventory system, estimated to total nearly 1.4 billion barrels when combining state-managed and commercial-social stockpiles.

The U.S. has not done much to adapt to the fluctuating oil market as Trump and his officials have remained largely optimistic about prices returning to normal as soon as the war ends, despite not having a set timeline for withdrawal. 

The president has hammered American companies like ExxonMobil and Chevron for making significant profit off the war through drilling efforts typically encouraged by his administration. 

“They’re making too much money. Too much money,” Trump said on Monday, urging them to decrease prices at the pump. 

“You’re surprised? I’m saying it. I’ll say it loud and clear,” the president added.

Despite his comments, major oil producers do not control most individual station prices and executives warn that global crude realities driven by the war with Iran will keep retail prices elevated.

Even when global crude benchmarks fluctuate or dip, retail prices at local stations historically lag behind by weeks.

data.title: Trump comes up short with Ogles in Tennessee: 3 takeaways from Thursday's primaries
data.description:
Voters in Tennessee dealt President Trump a blow and rejected Republican Rep. Andy Ogles at the polls Thursday.  

The second-term lawmaker faced a formidable primary challenge from Charlie Hatcher, a former state agriculture commissioner endorsed by outgoing Gov. Bill Lee (R). Hatcher’s victory is the latest blemish on Trump’s largely successful endorsement record this cycle. 

Thursday’s primaries also marked the first elections with the Volunteer State’s new House map after lawmakers approved GOP-friendly redistricting this spring.  

The state’s current House delegation includes eight Republicans and one Democrat, Rep. Steve Cohen. But GOP legislators redrew the map at Trump’s urging to create a 9-0 GOP edge after the Supreme Court issued its landmark decision dismantling a part of the Voting Rights Act this spring.  

Early voting alone in Shelby County, home to Memphis and now divided into three House districts, shows voters are engaged despite the changes to the congressional lines.  

Meanwhile, Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) looks to be one step closer to making history again in Tennessee after she won her GOP primary for the governor’s mansion.  

Here are the key takeaways from Tennessee’s primaries:  

Trump takes hit in fiery House primary 

Trump took a major hit in the newly drawn 5th Congressional District after his pick, Ogles, lost his primary. Charlie Hatcher is projected to secure the GOP nod, according to Decision Desk HQ.

The president attended a tele-rally for Ogles in late July, calling the House Republican “a terrific guy,”

This is the second House primary Trump has come up short in this week. On Tuesday, Republican Amir Hassan lost his race in Michigan’s 8th Congressional District to a candidate who previously dropped out of the race.  

Ogles has come under fire over some of his rhetoric over the years and faced outside opposition to his reelection bid in the 5th district, which extends outward from the state’s northwestern corner into a lobster-like figure in East and Middle Tennessee. 

The former Maury County mayor said that “Muslims don’t below in American society” in March and stated that “homosexuality has no place in America” in June.  

The congressman later said on the social platform X that a member of his communications team made the June post, calling the remarks “stupid, hurtful and a complete distraction from my America First focus.” He added that he “reprimanded” his aide. 

Meanwhile, Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, which is aligned with the clean energy sector, poured $2 million into the race to support Hatcher and attack Ogles. 

Ogles was also previously under investigation by the Justice Department over his campaign finances. Federal prosecutors backed off the probe, which began during the Biden era, in May, according to The Associated Press. 

DDHQ rates Ogles’ new seat as safely Republican, meaning Hatcher is expected to win the seat in November. 

Memphis posts strong early turnout after GOP redistricting  

Shelby County, home to Memphis, posted strong turnout numbers heading into the first primary elections since Republicans redrew the House map to favor the party in November.  

Blue-leaning Shelby County is currently separated into two congressional districts: the 8th and 9 districts. The 8th District is represented by GOP Rep. David Kustoff and voted for former Trump by 20 percentage points in 2024, according to The Downballot.  

Meanwhile, the 9th District, represented by Democratic Rep. Steve Cohen, voted for former Vice President Harris by 21 points in 2024.  

But the new map instituted in May split Shelby County into three districts — the 5th, 8th and 9th Districts, weakening the Democratic stronghold. All three districts are now rated as solidly Republican by Cook Political Report. 

Data from the Tennessee Secretary of State’s office showed that over 90,000 people — or a fifth of total registered voters in the county — voted early from July 17 to Aug. 1. This marks a 4 percent increase from 2022.  

More than 61,000 voters identified as Democrats while just shy of 28,000 registered as Republicans.  

While early Democratic turnout is historically higher in the region, the results show the party twice as engaged as the GOP in the county that will play a key role in three different congressional races.  

Kustoff ran unopposed Thursday, while Republican state Sen. Brent Taylor and Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson (D) won their respective primaries for Cohen’s seat. Hatcher is poised to face off against Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder, who is projected to win the Democratic primary in the 5th district.  

Blackburn on track to become state’s first woman governor 

Blackburn is one step closer to becoming Tennessee’s first woman governor after she defeated Rep. John Rose (R-Tenn.) and state Rep. Monty Fritts (R) in Thursday’s GOP primary.  

Trump notably declined to weigh in on the primary after backing both Blackburn and Rose in previous congressional bids. Blackburn will now take on Democrat Jerri Green, a Memphis City Council member, in November. 

Blackburn made history in 2018 when she was elected as Tennessee’s first woman senator.  

“From the bottom of my heart, thank you, Tennessee!” Blackburn wrote on X Thursday.  

“Tonight, I am humbled and honored that you’ve chosen me as your Republican nominee for Governor. Together, we’ve taken a major step toward that goal. I won’t let you down,” she added. “On to November.” 

Blackburn is almost certain to win the general election to succeed Lee, who is term limited, the state’s reliably red leanings. The Volunteer State hasn’t elected a Democrat for governor in two decades.

Democratic Gov. Phil Bredesen, who served as the state’s chief executive from 2003-2011, ran against Blackburn in the 2018 Senate race, losing by over 10 points.  

Blackburn’s Senate term is not up until 2030, and Tennessee law suggests the GOP senator could potentially pick her own replacement.  

“If a vacancy occurs in the office of United States senator, a successor shall be elected at the next regular November election and shall hold office until the term for which the predecessor was elected expires,” according to Tennessee code.  

“If the vacancy will deprive the state of its full representation at any time congress may be in session, the governor shall fill the vacancy by appointment until a successor is elected at the next regular November election and is qualified.”

data.title: Columbia mayor wins Democratic primary for Ogles seat in Tennessee
data.description:
Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder (D), one of three Democrats seeking to unseat Rep. Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.) and represent Tennessee’s 5th Congressional District, is projected to advance to facwe the incumbent in the November general election, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Molder won the Democratic primary against former educator Carrie Ann Iacomini, Memphis City Council member Yolanda Cooper-Sutton, writer Rachel Hurley and local activist Devante R. Hill.

The district went from being a likely win for Ogles, endorsed by President Trump and a fervent supporter of the president, to becoming solid red due to GOP-led redistricting, according to the nonpartisan Cook Political Report.

Democrats touting Molder suffered a blow when Gov. Bill Lee (R) approved the redrawn House map in May. The new map gives Ogles the edge over Molder, while Rep. Steve Cohen’s (D-Tenn.) 9th District shifts from solid Democrat to solid Republican.

Molder has significantly outraised Ogles, leading all candidates in fundraising with nearly $2.6 million, while Ogles raised over $600,000, according to the Federal Election Commission’s data.

Former Tennessee Gov. Phil Bredesen (D) endorsed Molder, telling voters in July that the district needs someone “focused on results, not theatrics.” He noted that “Chaz is a problem-solver” and a “uniter.”

“I’m ready for the Congress to ditch the theatrics and start doing something about the real challenges that face Tennesseans,” Bredesen said in his endorsement. “Especially the cost of groceries, housing and health care.”

Cohen and former Rep. Jim Cooper (D-Tenn.), who both represented parts of Memphis and Nashville before the recent GOP-led redistricting battle, as well as the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, have endorsed Molder.

Molder told Action News 5, a Memphis-based news outlet, in July that he was initially angry about Lee approving the legislature’s new congressional map.

“But then when I realized that I had an opportunity to represent places like Ripley, Tennessee, places like Martin, places like Franklin and then places like Memphis, a city that I know and love so well, this really was all of a sudden very exciting for me,” he said, adding that he would be “a champion for all of the counties in our district and frankly, for all of Tennessee.”
